item.title: "You suck": Emmer unloads on Senate Republicans
item.description:
House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) is saying out loud what House Republicans have been grumbling about for much of the year: They're fed up with the Senate.

Why it matters You won't ever hear Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) or Majority Leader Steve Scalise (R-La.) talk about their Senate counterparts like this.

  • "There are no Democrats. There are no Republicans. They are just senators," Emmer told donors last week at a closed-door fundraiser Axios attended for Rep. Mark Harris (R-N.C.).
  • Emmer said Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) "is doing the job that he thinks he's supposed to do. There's a certain fraternity sorority that is the U.S. Senate."

The intrigue: Emmer had a blunt message for senators who repeatedly say they can't pass House GOP priorities: "Don't just keep telling me 'Don't have the votes. Don't have the votes.' You suck."

  • Emmer said he once thought as a House member that he should stay out of the filibuster debate. Now, he thinks his colleagues should "get rid of the darn filibuster."
  • A Senate GOP aide retorted that what would "suck" would be losing the majority and that Republicans should be targeting Democrats instead of attacking their own side.

Driving the news: Emmer's comments are the most critical yet from a House GOP leader, but sum up the mood inside the conference.

  • More than a dozen Republicans paralyzed the House floor this summer in an effort to force Senate action on the SAVE America Act, the GOP's signature election bill that's become a major source of tension between the two chambers.
  • "We're frustrated with the Senate," Emmer told Axios in an interview after the fundraiser. "We feel like we've been doing everything we were hired to do, and a lot of it goes over to the Senate and it just sits there."
  • House Republicans put their votes "up on the board," Emmer argued, while senators "try to avoid" taking tough votes.

The big picture: House GOP leaders often say they've "done their job" when asked about unfinished business. But there's a clear implication in that phrase: The Senate hasn't.

  • Johnson has pointed to the backlog across the Capitol — including when he defended sending the House home early last month by noting that hundreds of House-passed bills were awaiting Senate action.
  • The speaker blames Democrats for that, but his complaints have put the spotlight on Senate GOP leadership.

Zoom in: Congressional Republicans spent much of the summer on completely different wavelengths over reconciliation 3.0, which doesn't require any Democratic votes.

  • Johnson pushed the Senate to take up the House's reconciliation framework, declaring in July that the Senate would pass it before leaving for August recess.
  • "That'd be news to me," Thune said at the time about Johnson's floated timeline. The Senate left town without any action on reconciliation 3.0.
  • "They can say all day long, you know, 'It's going to be hard.' Everything's hard. Give me a lecture about how hard things are. That's what I do every day. They've got to figure out a way to get it done," Scalise told Axios of his colleagues in the Senate in July.

The bottom line: Emmer stopped short of saying Senate Republicans have been a bigger obstacle to the GOP agenda than Democrats.

  • But he said two things frustrate lawmakers in the House when it comes to Senate Republicans: 1) They don't say what changes would get them to yes; and 2) they don't put themselves on the record when the answer is no.
  • "Put your money where your mouth is. Put your vote up on the board, and let's see where you really are," Emmer told Axios.

item.title: House GOP leaders admit redistricting fell short
item.description:
House GOP leaders are now openly acknowledging that their mid-decade redistricting push didn't work out as well as they'd hoped.

Why it matters: Republicans kicked off the redistricting wars hoping new maps would give them a bigger cushion against the historical headwinds facing the president's party.

  • That advantage is looking a lot smaller than they envisioned.

Driving the news: House Majority Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) told Axios that Republicans won't win all 13 seats they'd hoped to gain from new maps.

  • "We're not gonna win all 13 of those redistricted seats. That's correct. We're not," Emmer told Axios aboard a plane Thursday between campaign stops in North Carolina and Virginia.
  • Emmer echoed House Republican Conference Chair Lisa McClain (R-Mich.), who told Axios last month that Republicans were unlikely to sweep all 13.

Zoom in: Emmer said he'd be "surprised" if Republicans sweep all five newly drawn seats in Texas and "shocked" if they win all four in Florida.

  • But he said Republicans are certain to pick up newly drawn seats in Alabama, Louisiana and Tennessee.
  • At a fundraiser for Rep. Mark Harris (R-N.C.) on Thursday, Emmer told donors that Republicans could also offset losses with pickups in Maine and potentially North Carolina, Ohio, New Mexico and Washington.
  • Even assuming Republicans lose five seats because of redistricting in California and Utah, pickups elsewhere give the party a path to come out ahead, Emmer told donors.

State of play: Redistricting still gave Republicans an edge, just smaller than they once thought.

  • The Cook Political Report now projects Republicans will net around four seats from redistricting alone, down from the double-digit gains Republicans once hoped to squeeze from new maps.
  • Democrats' maps in California and Utah — in response to a new Texas map — offset the GOP gains. Some newly drawn Republican pickup opportunities have become more competitive than expected.

The bottom line: Democrats need to net just three seats to win the House, and the broader battlefield is moving in their direction.

  • Cook shifted 15 House races toward Democrats last month, while Sabato's Crystal Ball moved 11 races toward Democrats days later.
  • Many of the most competitive races are now in districts President Trump carried in 2024.

item.title: CDC: Monitoring Russian plague risk, "prepared" for any threat
item.description:
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says it is monitoring reports of a suspected pneumonic plague case in Russia and says it is prepared for any threat that emerges.

Why it matters: Pneumonic plague is the most dangerous form of plague and is almost always fatal unless if left untreated.

The latest: President Trump told reporters Tuesday that he has a call scheduled with Russian leader Vladimir Putin to discuss the suspected plague case and would speak with him "very soon."

  • Asked what U.S. intelligence was saying about the situation, Trump said officials were in "very deep discussions" and that "we'll be able to report about it, probably tomorrow."

Catch up quick: Darya Shipilova, a worker at a Russian anti-plague institute, died after reports that she may have been exposed to plague bacteria while working at the Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia.

  • Russian authorities say testing has not linked her death to plague or to pathogens she handled at work.
  • However, at least five hospitals in the area remain in quarantine and almost 200 people who had contact with Shipilova have been placed under medical observation as a precaution.

What they're saying: "We are working across the U.S. government to assess developments as additional information becomes available," the CDC said in an X post Tuesday.

  • "At this time, there is no indication of a broader threat to the United States, but CDC and our interagency partners are prepared and will continue to monitor the situation closely."

Context: The CDC said the plague is a dangerous bacterial disease that can be treated with antibiotics, especially when caught early.

  • Pneumonic plague can spread between people through respiratory droplets during close contact.
  • The CDC says "rapid identification and treatment of infected individuals, and monitoring of potentially exposed individuals" are important for keeping people safe.

State of play: The concerns have drawn attention on social media and from government officials and the White House.

  • President Trump acknowledged Monday that he is aware of the situation. "We just heard about it," Trump told reporters Monday, but said he hadn't spoken to Russian President Vladimir Putin about it yet.
  • "We'll help them," Trump said. "We'll help them as much as we can."
  • The Department of Health and Human Services and the State Department are also monitoring the situation.

What we're watching: Secretary of State Marco Rubio called on Russia Tuesday to share more information about Shipilova's death, per Reuters.

  • ​Rubio told reporters: "I ​think it's incumbent upon Russia to obviously ⁠share more information with the world."

Editor's note: This story has been updated with comment from President Trump.

item.title: A brutal winter heating bill is coming for some homes
item.description:
Americans could pay far more to heat their homes with oil this winter than last, a new analysis reviewed by Axios shows, as volatile energy markets and the Iran War deepen the affordability crisis.

Why it matters: Heating bills are eating into household budgets before winter sets in, with stark divides between fuel types.

By the numbers: Families that heat with oil could pay about 50% more this winter than last, according to estimates from the National Energy Assistance Directors Association (NEADA), up from its 31.3% projection in mid-September.

  • The average cost of heating a home with oil is expected to rise by about $878, costing over $2,600 this winter.
  • By comparison, the Energy Information Administration's Winter Fuels Outlook released Tuesday projects electricity bills will rise 4% nationally, while natural gas bills will fall 9% and propane spending will drop 3%. EIA expects a smaller increase on heating oil than NEADA, projecting a 21% increase in household expenditures.

Northeastern households will feel the pain most acutely: about 82% of home heating oil is consumed in the region, where some states lack robust natural gas pipelines, according to NEADA data.

  • Just 3% of U.S. households use oil as their primary heat source, compared to about 45% using natural gas and 43% using electricity, NEADA says.

The big picture: Heating oil prices are rising as global oil markets falter because of the wars in Iran and Ukraine and as refinery activity declines.

  • "Those trends really reflect the worst-case scenario of this war, and they are going to feel it this winter, and it's unfortunate," Mark Wolfe, executive director of the NEADA, tells Axios.

What they're saying: Because of the cost, some families will cut back on food or medicine, borrow from payday lenders, or turn the heat down to unsafe levels to cover their heating bills, Wolfe says.

  • "With low-income families, sometimes states will move money around to help them, but they'll go without," Wolfe says.

Between the lines: States can put more money toward heating assistance, but they have fewer tools to protect heating-oil customers than households served by regulated gas and electric utilities, Wolfe says.

  • States can require utilities to offer discounts, affordability programs or winter shutoff protections, but they generally don't apply to independent heating-oil dealers.

Zoom in: Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey declared a State of Energy Emergency Monday over rising winter energy costs, unlocking nearly $150 million in relief and expanding assistance to middle-class households that heat with oil.

  • Rhode Island has also declared an energy affordability emergency and directed $28 million in reserves toward winter electric-bill relief, and Maine Gov. Janet Mills announced $40 million in automatically applied electricity discounts for low-income residents.

Zoom out: The energy affordability crisis is compounded by the Trump administration's attempts to dismantle the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, or LIHEAP.

  • The administration fired LIHEAP's federal staff at the Department of Health and Human Services in April 2025 and proposed eliminating funding for the program.
  • LIHEAP is still running, but state administrators are operating without dedicated federal staff.
  • The White House referred Axios to HHS, which said it "will carry out its responsibilities for funding Congress has made available" and that "HHS has the staff and capacity to distribute these funds in a timely manner."

The bottom line: Winter is coming, and Americans need to prepare for both the cold — and the prices — to bite.

Go deeper: How to save money on your electric bill this winter

item.title: Trump's PAC won't pay taxpayers back for his ads
item.description:
President Trump's super PAC will not reimburse the government for taxpayer money spent on campaign-style ads promoting the administration.

Why it matters: Taxpayers have footed a multimillion-dollar bill for the advertisements, which some critics of the president have called "government propaganda."

What they're saying: "The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," Trump wrote on Truth Social Monday evening.

  • "This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc," he wrote, referring to a super PAC affiliated with the president.

Worth noting: Federal law generally bars federal officeholders from directing spending decisions for super PACs.

Zoom in: When reached for comment, a White House spokesperson told Axios that Trump's announcement "was not referring to reimbursement."

Catch up quick: The White House previously defended the ads as "public service announcements" that are "clearly not political."

  • The White House says the ads are instead meant to be patriotic, noting that Trump isn't on the ballot this year.
  • Nonetheless, one such ad repurposes a nearly identical ad from Trump's 2024 presidential campaign, cutting it shorter and adding "Paid for by the U.S. government."

Zoom out: The ads, which have run on cable and network television, including during NFL games, have cost at least $11 million since September, according to an AdImpact analysis conducted by the AP.

  • The spots were paid for through a $20 million Department of Homeland Security contract.

Go deeper: Scoop: Trump's hand-picked, taxpayer-funded ads about to ramp up

item.title: DOJ moves to strip citizenship from 40 people
item.description:
President Trump's Justice Department moved to revoke citizenship from 40 naturalized citizens accused of crimes in recent months, representing what Attorney General Todd Blanche called the "largest denaturalization effort in modern history."

The big picture: The Trump administration has made denaturalization a priority, moving personnel to pursue more cases and setting a goal of 250 cases by this month.

Driving the news: The DOJ filed 40 denaturalization actions in district courts spanning coast to coast between Aug. 21 and Oct. 2, according to a Monday statement.

  • "Every single one of these individuals lied their way into U.S. citizenship," Assistant Attorney General Brett Shumate said in a statement.

Context: Denaturalization cases have a high burden of proof, and to revoke someone's citizenship, the DOJ must file a revocation action in federal district court.

  • The general grounds for revocation, per U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, are illegal procurement of naturalized citizenship or lying to get it.
  • "For civil revocation of naturalization, the burden of proof is clear, convincing, and unequivocal evidence which does not leave the issue in doubt," per USCIS.

Zoom in: Individuals named in Monday's statement had been convicted of or pleaded guilty to an array of offenses, including conspiracy to commit money laundering, sexual abuse of a minor and aggravated sodomy.

What we're watching: The DOJ did not immediately respond to Axios' request for specifics on how many actions had been filed since the start of the second Trump administration.

  • In April, the New York Times reported that the DOJ had identified 384 foreign-born Americans whose citizenship the department wanted to revoke.
  • The following month, Axios' Brittany Gibson reported that USCIS lawyers had been temporarily moved to U.S. attorneys' offices to work on denaturalization cases.

Go deeper: Birthright citizenship decision gives advocates short-lived sigh of relief

item.title: AI tools flood into underground cybercrime markets
item.description:
Hackers in underground cybercriminal forums are on shopping sprees for new AI tools, according to research shared first with Axios.

Why it matters: AI is making once-specialized hacking capabilities cheaper and easier to buy, potentially transforming far more criminals into dangerous hackers.

By the numbers: Advertisements for AI tools on underground forums and platforms surged from fewer than 50 per month in late 2025 to more than 1,400 by February, according to a report from Halcyon's Ransomware Research Center.

  • Sellers offered access to ChatGPT Plus accounts for as little as 10 cents and jailbreak prompts to trick models into breaking their safeguards for 32 cents, per the research.
  • Halcyon studied nearly 4,000 posts across 77 Telegram channels, 20 dark web forums and five specialized underground markets between October and May.

Threat level: Companies are already losing millions of dollars to the types of cyberattacks enabled by the tools found on these underground markets.

  • "It really goes to show you how cheap it is to conduct these activities ... which should be scary for organizations," Cynthia Kaiser, head of Halcyon's Ransomware Research Center and former deputy director of FBI Cyber, told Axios.

The big picture: Cybercriminals have completely commercialized the sale and creation of these tools, often modeling software-as-a-service subscription models and online storefronts, per the report.

  • Some sellers are now offering AI tools they tested and promoted on traditional dark web forums through easier-to-manage storefronts hosted on Telegram.
  • "It shouldn't have been shocking to me," Kaiser said. "But what we should take away from this is also how much cybercriminals have learned throughout the years about how to sell and package — and they applied this really quickly to the AI models."

Zoom in: Hackers are selling four types of AI tools:

  • Jailbroken and stolen AI services, including prompts that allow users to strip the safety guardrails from mainstream models for as little as $10.
  • Identity fraud and phishing tools that make impersonating real people quick and easy.
  • Access to models trained on malicious data to aid cybercrime, such as the popular WormGPT that's designed to write phishing emails and malware.
  • AI-augmented malware and infrastructure, including a system that can call as many as 120 people at once as part of a scam operation.

Flashback: In 2023, hackers could only tap a handful of one-off tools. Now, there's a robust marketplace.

  • Still, AI is largely helping criminals perform discrete elements of existing attacks more cheaply and efficiently, Kaiser said.
  • "What you're not seeing for sale is an agent that does it all for you and has this amazing success rate," she said.

What to watch: Halcyon didn't find evidence of criminals selling AI systems capable of running fully autonomous cyberattacks.

  • Even in AI-enabled malware and infrastructure, Kaiser said, much of what researchers are seeing involves coding assistance, infrastructure and other individual tasks rather than AI creating and deploying malware on its own.

Go deeper: Rogue AI agents expose internet's frail foundation
item.content:encoded:
Hackers in underground cybercriminal forums are on shopping sprees for new AI tools, according to research shared first with Axios.

Why it matters: AI is making once-specialized hacking capabilities cheaper and easier to buy, potentially transforming far more criminals into dangerous hackers.

By the numbers: Advertisements for AI tools on underground forums and platforms surged from fewer than 50 per month in late 2025 to more than 1,400 by February, according to a report from Halcyon's Ransomware Research Center.

  • Sellers offered access to ChatGPT Plus accounts for as little as 10 cents and jailbreak prompts to trick models into breaking their safeguards for 32 cents, per the research.
  • Halcyon studied nearly 4,000 posts across 77 Telegram channels, 20 dark web forums and five specialized underground markets between October and May.

Threat level: Companies are already losing millions of dollars to the types of cyberattacks enabled by the tools found on these underground markets.

  • "It really goes to show you how cheap it is to conduct these activities ... which should be scary for organizations," Cynthia Kaiser, head of Halcyon's Ransomware Research Center and former deputy director of FBI Cyber, told Axios.

The big picture: Cybercriminals have completely commercialized the sale and creation of these tools, often modeling software-as-a-service subscription models and online storefronts, per the report.

  • Some sellers are now offering AI tools they tested and promoted on traditional dark web forums through easier-to-manage storefronts hosted on Telegram.
  • "It shouldn't have been shocking to me," Kaiser said. "But what we should take away from this is also how much cybercriminals have learned throughout the years about how to sell and package — and they applied this really quickly to the AI models."

Zoom in: Hackers are selling four types of AI tools:

  • Jailbroken and stolen AI services, including prompts that allow users to strip the safety guardrails from mainstream models for as little as $10.
  • Identity fraud and phishing tools that make impersonating real people quick and easy.
  • Access to models trained on malicious data to aid cybercrime, such as the popular WormGPT that's designed to write phishing emails and malware.
  • AI-augmented malware and infrastructure, including a system that can call as many as 120 people at once as part of a scam operation.

Flashback: In 2023, hackers could only tap a handful of one-off tools. Now, there's a robust marketplace.

  • Still, AI is largely helping criminals perform discrete elements of existing attacks more cheaply and efficiently, Kaiser said.
  • "What you're not seeing for sale is an agent that does it all for you and has this amazing success rate," she said.

What to watch: Halcyon didn't find evidence of criminals selling AI systems capable of running fully autonomous cyberattacks.

  • Even in AI-enabled malware and infrastructure, Kaiser said, much of what researchers are seeing involves coding assistance, infrastructure and other individual tasks rather than AI creating and deploying malware on its own.

item.title: Paramount closes historic $110B deal for Warner Bros. Discovery to create Skydance
item.description:
Paramount Skydance on Tuesday closed its deal to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery, ending a dramatic, yearlong process that rattled Hollywood, Wall Street and Washington.

Why it matters: The deal creates one of the largest entertainment behemoths in the world and makes David Ellison — a lesser-known figure outside of Hollywood — one of the most powerful people in culture and business.

Zoom in: The combined entity, rebranded Skydance, will house three major movie studios (Paramount Pictures, Warner Bros. Pictures and Skydance), two global streamers (Paramount+ and HBO Max) and two major news networks (CNN and CBS).

  • It will also create a cable juggernaut, marrying Paramount's Viacom channels, such as MTV, VH1 and Comedy Central, with WBD's cable networks, including TBS, TNT, Food Network and Discovery.
  • The combination of those assets on the back end won't all be felt by consumers, but product changes are coming. The combined company, for example, plans to merge HBO Max and Paramount + into one giant unified streamer.

The big picture: The transaction forced the entertainment industry and regulators around the world to confront how much consolidation is necessary for traditional media companies to compete with Big Tech.

  • While some countries took a closer look at the deal than others, every government that required regulatory approval for the merger ultimately blessed the transaction.
  • Although Netflix did meaningfully engage in a bidding war for WBD, it eventually abandoned its interest when the asset became too pricey.

Reality check: Merger fights don't typically enter the zeitgeist for everyday Americans, but this one played into a broader societal debate around the concentration of power among the elite and the independence of federal regulators.

  • Ellison's father, Oracle co-founder and Trump ally Larry Ellison, agreed to backstop billions of dollars of equity financing to seal the deal.
  • Federal regulators cleared billions of dollars in equity investments from Middle Eastern sovereign wealth funds to support the deal. The Federal Communications Commission, led by Trump ally Brendan Carr, granted Paramount's request to exceed foreign ownership limits for broadcasters.

Between the lines: The political tension surrounding the deal was on full display when a dozen Democratic state attorneys general sued to block the transaction as it approached the finish line this summer.

  • The state AGs said their case was rooted in traditional antitrust law around film and cable dominance, not politics.
  • But after a settlement was announced clearing the deal, at least one participating state attorney general admitted that they wanted the agreement to force a divestiture of CBS and CNN.

State of play: To alleviate regulatory concerns about the enormous concentration of assets, Skydance made a slew of commitments in its settlement, including theatrical film release minimums and investments in domestic production jobs.

  • But the creative industry is still on edge as it anticipates a potentially huge number of job cuts as a result of the merger.

What to watch: The deal, which is one of the most highly levered transactions in American history, will test the market's appetite for megamergers financed by huge amounts of debt amid rising interest rates.

  • To get the transaction over the finish line, Paramount raised $52 billion in new debt, per Bloomberg. Some of that debt is very expensive, carrying a yield of nearly 9%.
  • In addition to the debt it raised, Skydance will carry WBD's existing liabilities, totaling $87.5 billion in debt, according to Fitch Ratings.
Data: Financial Modeling Prep; Chart: Christine Wang/Axios

The bottom line: Ellison has proven himself to be one of the most savvy dealmakers in American history. His next test is whether he can build a sustainable business from a mountain of debt.

item.title: SF Fed president: AI demand could extend energy shock
item.description:
Some companies are preparing for an AI-fueled chip squeeze that could push up prices far beyond the data center boom alone, Mary Daly, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, tells Axios.

Why it matters: The Fed can usually look through supply shocks that come and go. Daly's concern is that AI, tariffs and higher energy costs could last longer than expected or compound each other — keeping inflation elevated and requiring more tightening.

State of play: Daly says AI demand could spread beyond high-end chips before supply catches up, extending the shock beyond the period the Fed would normally expect to look through.

  • "I see it less as a one-off," she says, referring to AI-driven pressure on chip and other technology prices.
  • Daly says the Fed typically thinks in terms of shocks fading within one to three years. "This is probably further out before we get relief."
  • "It doesn't seem like the demand for AI is going down. If anything, it seems like it's going up."

Zoom in: Daly's district includes Silicon Valley and many of the companies driving the AI boom. In conversations with business contacts, she says, she's starting to hear signs that companies are bracing for tighter chip supplies — suggesting that the AI boom is beginning to alter purchasing and product-design decisions outside the data center sector.

  • Daly says that some firms are seeking forward contracts for memory chips "so that they know they have a supplier."
  • Those contracts can give companies more certainty about future supply — a notable development in the memory sector, a fast-depreciating market where firms typically have less reason to lock in chips ahead of time.
  • Daly says some companies are also beginning to "reengineer their products" to rely less on chips, giving them more room to maneuver in case supplies tighten.
  • "I see that as a signal that there is a little bit of concern this is going to spread more broadly."

What to watch: The fear is that the scramble for AI hardware begins competing with the chips used in cars, appliances and other goods — recreating some of the bottlenecks that drove prices higher after the pandemic, Daly says.

  • She points to autos after the pandemic, when chip shortages left manufacturers unable to finish vehicles and pushed prices higher.
  • The risk now is that demand for AI-specific equipment spills into the broader semiconductor market, raising costs for companies with little connection to data centers.

Friction point: The Fed could face an awkward problem as AI-driven price pressures spread. The companies fueling the boom are also among the least sensitive to higher interest rates.

  • "These hyperscalers aren't very interest rate-sensitive," Daly says, though she notes they could become more so as they increasingly rely on borrowing to finance the AI buildout.
  • Daly says the biggest AI spending numbers are concentrated among hyperscalers, but plenty of other companies investing in the technology are more sensitive to borrowing costs.
  • That means higher rates can still restrain the broader economy and inflation outlook, even if they do less to slow the firms at the center of the boom.
  • "I do think tightening policy has an effect on the outlook for inflation," Daly says.

The bottom line: The AI boom is emerging as a fresh inflation risk for the Fed — one that could spread through supply chains, linger for years and prove more difficult to cool with higher interest rates.

Daly affirmed her support for the Fed's interest rate hike three weeks ago, and, as has become the norm among top officials, declined to say much about whether she advocates further action.

  • But she did give a sense of what will shape her view: whether the energy, trade and other shocks that have pushed up inflation this year show signs of abating.

What they're saying: "I was very pleased, very supportive of the rate hike we took in September," Daly says. "It seemed completely necessary at this juncture to respond to the fact that inflation risks have gone up."

  • "Whether more will be needed depends on the same set of conditions ... that I mentioned," she says.
  • "If the shocks that we've experienced — tariffs, oil prices from the Middle East conflict, and then AI — if they prove to be conventional shocks where they come, they go, and they have temporary effects, then we may not need more. And I still have some probability on that."
  • "But if they either compound each other or they just simply last longer than we had forecast that they would ... if we have a second round of tariff negotiations that result in more tariffs, then that would be a second shock on top of a first shock. That would extend the period of time over which those shocks would play out."

She later added that the Fed's policy committee, the FOMC, is "not going to lose track of the labor market, and we're going to continue to be careful in our deliberations so that we can really dissect whether those shocks are going to roll off or whether they're going to compound, and whether we think that underlying inflation is gaining momentum or it's not."

Of note: This framing differs from a view that monetary policy is out of whack with the broader state of the economy and needs adjustment, as heard from some of the more hawkish voices on the committee.

  • Daly's argument implies openness to being done with rate hikes if geopolitical events cooperate in the coming weeks and months.

By contrast, some of her colleagues see an economy with broader inflationary forces at play that compel an adjustment to the monetary dials.

  • "In my view, given changes to the economy, we were out of position, and we made an adjustment in the right direction," Fed governor Michael Barr said last month.

item.title: Trump remarks that Iran could "take out" Los Angeles, San Diego draw backlash
item.description:
California leaders blasted President Trump after he said during a Monday rally about Iran, "Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego."

The big picture: The backlash — and the White House's insistence that Trump was misunderstood — underscored the ambiguity of his meandering speech: An argument that the war was worth enduring to protect Americans came out sounding like an invitation to attack two U.S. cities.

  • An administration account posted on X that Trump meant that the U.S. was fighting Iran to "STOP Iran from having the ability to take out LA and San Diego."

Driving the news: Faced with an unpopular war and stubbornly high gas prices, Trump seemingly argued that the current economic pain is "a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe" during his Nebraska rally.

  • "It's a small price to pay for keeping the world safe, keeping our country safe," he said. "They can take out a city. Let them take, let it — let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego. That's — this is a very small price to pay, and it's gonna be over very soon."

Friction point: The comment received swift backlash from Golden State leaders:

  • California Gov. Gavin Newsom wrote, "After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should "take out" Los Angeles and San Diego. He is deranged and dangerous."
  • San Diego Mayor Todd Gloria also admonished the president, writing, "San Diego is not collateral damage. We are not expendable."
  • And LA Mayor Karen Bass responded, "His statements against our city are dangerous and could potentially compromise our safety. The role of a president is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives."

Between the lines: Analysts online perceived his comments in various ways, with some noting his circuitous language could have masked his true intent.

  • But others reeled at the plain text of the comments from the president, who in the past has suggested using "dangerous" U.S. cities as military "training grounds."
  • The White House pointed Axios to a post from Communications Director Steven Cheung, who argued the president "was clearly stating U.S. cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn't been stopped.

Context: Military bases across San Diego employ more than 136,000 active duty members and civilians, according to a 2025 report from the San Diego Military Advisory Council.

  • Rep. Scott Peters (D), who represents the city, noted those deep military roots in his statement condemning the president's words, writing, "San Diego is a proud military town, home to 115,000 courageous active duty servicemembers and their families. Military service is at the root of our community and culture."

Go deeper: After nixing Iran proposal, Trump tells Axios he expects talks this week

item.title: "I don't want an oligopoly": New open-weight AI models mount a comeback against China
item.description:
A new crop of powerful, Western open-weight AI systems are mounting a comeback, with fresh models from Reflection and Mistral narrowing China's recent lead.

Why it matters: These models and others will give businesses and governments alternatives to the closed ecosystems of OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as to Chinese options they may have eschewed for security reasons.

  • But putting powerful model weights into the world also makes their safeguards easier to remove, a concern that's growing as models become more capable in areas like cybersecurity.

What they're saying: Both companies are arguing that raw intelligence isn't the only way to measure the AI race, and they present the notion of user control as a core opportunity and selling point.

  • "Once you're spending that amount on intelligence, you want to move from renting it to owning it yourself," Reflection CEO Misha Laskin told Axios. "That's kind of where open source is very powerful because it is customizable at every level."
  • Mistral VP of science Pierre Stock said the themes he repeatedly hears from customers include control over data and intellectual property, business continuity, the ability to customize models and cost.
  • "I don't want to live in the future in which any oligopoly controls closed access to this type of intelligence," Stock said in an interview.

Zoom in: Reflection on Monday introduced Beam, a 501-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model, with 23 billion parameters active at a time.

  • Reflection says Beam is competitive with China's GLM-5.2 and approaches Alibaba's Qwen 3.8-Max on some coding and agentic tasks. Its own published benchmarks show a mixed picture: Beam beats or roughly matches the Chinese models on some tests while trailing them on others.
  • Reflection says Beam can achieve reasoning performance comparable to GLM-5.2 with three to four times less computing firepower — an important consideration because the cost of running AI models is now as important to many customers as raw performance.
  • Reflection plans to release Beam's weights later this month, along with tools for running, evaluating and fine-tuning it.

Meanwhile, Mistral said Tuesday it is finishing work on a new flagship model, Mistral Large 4, aka "Le Chonk." It's a 1-trillion-parameter multimodal model with 49 billion active parameters, trained on 4,000 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs over two months in Mistral's own European data centers.

  • Stock told Axios the company believes Le Chonk is the world's best open-weight model and said it can outperform closed models on certain tasks.
  • But Stock acknowledged that Mistral hasn't yet caught the leading closed models. "We're not there yet on the frontier," he said.
  • Mistral is initially making the model available through a moderated API, with a version with fewer restrictions and broader cybersecurity capabilities being shared with select partners for testing. It plans to release the weights Oct. 27 after further reinforcement learning and safety testing.

The big picture: Chinese companies including Alibaba, Z.ai, Moonshot and DeepSeek have driven much of the recent momentum in open-weight AI.

  • The arrival of competitive models from Reflection and Mistral suggests Western labs may be narrowing a gap that had begun to look structural.

Yes, but: The same characteristic that gives customers control over an open-weight model also limits the developer's control over how it is used.

  • Once weights are publicly available, users can modify the model, including attempting to remove safeguards added by its creator.
  • That's particularly significant as models become more capable at cybersecurity and other potentially dangerous tasks.

The other side: Mistral and Reflection argue that openness can also improve safety.

  • Laskin said having a larger ecosystem able to inspect models and hunt for vulnerabilities is safer than concentrating that work among a few hundred researchers inside closed labs. He said there should nevertheless be capability-based safety thresholds that determine whether any model — open or closed — should be released.
  • Stock acknowledged a trade-off in releasing weights but argued that making capable models available can accelerate cyber defenses and allow outside researchers to audit the technology. Mistral is using a staged release to give itself additional time for testing.
  • Open-weight models also ensure that those defending against cyberattacks have adequate tools. "If we open weight as many models as possible, including ML4 — which is among the best models in the world on cyber — then you accelerate the defense part way more," Stock said.

  • "I don't want to live in the future in which any oligopoly controls closed access to this type of intelligence," Stock said in an interview.

Zoom in: Reflection on Monday introduced Beam, a 501-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model, with 23 billion parameters active at a time.

  • Reflection says Beam is competitive with China's GLM-5.2 and approaches Alibaba's Qwen 3.8-Max on some coding and agentic tasks. Its own published benchmarks show a mixed picture: Beam beats or roughly matches the Chinese models on some tests while trailing them on others.
  • Reflection says Beam can achieve reasoning performance comparable to GLM-5.2 with three to four times less computing firepower — an important consideration because the cost of running AI models is now as important to many customers as raw performance.
  • Reflection plans to release Beam's weights later this month, along with tools for running, evaluating and fine-tuning it.

Meanwhile, Mistral said Tuesday it is finishing work on a new flagship model, Mistral Large 4, aka "Le Chonk." It's a 1-trillion-parameter multimodal model with 49 billion active parameters, trained on 4,000 Nvidia Grace Blackwell GPUs over two months in Mistral's own European data centers.

  • Stock told Axios the company believes Le Chonk is the world's best open-weight model and said it can outperform closed models on certain tasks.
  • But Stock acknowledged that Mistral hasn't yet caught the leading closed models. "We're not there yet on the frontier," he said.
  • Mistral is initially making the model available through a moderated API, with a version with fewer restrictions and broader cybersecurity capabilities being shared with select partners for testing. It plans to release the weights Oct. 27 after further reinforcement learning and safety testing.

The big picture: Chinese companies including Alibaba, Z.ai, Moonshot and DeepSeek have driven much of the recent momentum in open-weight AI.

  • The arrival of competitive models from Reflection and Mistral suggests Western labs may be narrowing a gap that had begun to look structural.

Yes, but: The same characteristic that gives customers control over an open-weight model also limits the developer's control over how it is used.

  • Once weights are publicly available, users can modify the model, including attempting to remove safeguards added by its creator.
  • That's particularly significant as models become more capable at cybersecurity and other potentially dangerous tasks.

The other side: Mistral and Reflection argue that openness can also improve safety.

  • Laskin said having a larger ecosystem able to inspect models and hunt for vulnerabilities is safer than concentrating that work among a few hundred researchers inside closed labs. He said there should nevertheless be capability-based safety thresholds that determine whether any model — open or closed — should be released.
  • Stock acknowledged a trade-off in releasing weights but argued that making capable models available can accelerate cyber defenses and allow outside researchers to audit the technology. Mistral is using a staged release to give itself additional time for testing.
  • Open-weight models also ensure that those defending against cyberattacks have adequate tools. "If we open weight as many models as possible, including ML4 — which is among the best models in the world on cyber — then you accelerate the defense part way more," Stock said.

item.title: The midterms are an energy election — and here are five places to look
item.description:
Scratch the surface of the year's biggest stories — the Iran war and AI — and both are bound up in the costs of energy.

Why it matters: Prices for gasoline, diesel and power are playing a prominent role in some of the tightest races for control of Congress.

  • The war has kept gasoline prices way above $4 per gallon for months, and helped push diesel to record highs.
  • Fairly or unfairly, data centers are getting blamed for rising electricity prices.
  • It's all unfolding as affordability more broadly tops the agenda in races nationwide.

Here's a look at how energy politics are playing out in five critical contests...

Senate

Michigan. Power prices climbed faster than the national average over the past year in the Wolverine state, and data centers surfaced early in the Democratic primary and stayed prominent in the tight general election race.

  • Former GOP Rep. Mike Rogers' campaign shows how Republican hopefuls are willing to split with President Trump on energy and AI — or at least get ahead of him.
  • Rogers called for a one-year moratorium on data centers in August. And he called for a temporary ban on diesel exports in September, an idea Trump then flirted with but backed off.
  • On the Democratic side, if Abdul El-Sayed's January "terms of engagement" for data centers looks familiar, it's because it reflects an increasingly common Democratic view around community buy-in and clean energy.

Ohio. AI's voracious appetite for electricity is fueling the clash between Republican Sen. Jon Husted and Democrat Sherrod Brown.

  • Husted has made the case that data centers — not households — should pay for the new power plants and grid infrastructure needed to serve them. A bill he sponsored aimed at doing that fell short in the Senate after passing the House overwhelmingly.
  • Brown is attacking Husted for previously championing data centers and tax incentives to attract them to Ohio.
  • The fight encapsulates a broader question surrounding the AI boom: Who should pay for the massive buildout needed to power it?

Alaska. The Iran war is turning energy prices into a potent issue in the race between Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola.

  • In rural communities, fuel already costs far more than in the Lower 48, with gasoline reaching $10 a gallon in some places. Peltola is tying rising fuel costs directly to Sullivan's support for the war, arguing higher diesel prices are hammering fishermen and families.
  • Sullivan has called for temporarily halting U.S. diesel exports and argues Alaska should produce more of its own energy.
  • Looming over it all is Trump's push for a massive Alaska project to export liquefied natural gas.

House

Colorado 8th. This is a contest where energy could be the tipping point. Both general elections in the district's young history have been decided by less than 1%, and energy is prominent this time around.

  • One thing to watch is how much political cover a recent data center vote gives incumbent Republican Gabe Evans.
  • Evans' bipartisan Ratepayer Protection Act passed the House 417-3 last month. It urges states — but doesn't force them — to set rules ensuring data center developers cover generation and grid upgrade costs
  • Don't sleep on gasoline either. New Democratic ads supporting challenger Manny Rutinel tie Evans to Trump's war with Iran and higher gasoline prices.

Pennsylvania 8th. Data centers have become a central issue in the House race between Republican Rep. Rob Bresnahan and Democratic Scranton Mayor Paige Cognetti.

  • Northeastern Pennsylvania is fielding proposals for the energy-hungry facilities. Cognetti is campaigning explicitly against projects that raise electric bills, threaten water supplies or receive tax breaks.
  • Bresnahan, who has previously supported data center development, has introduced legislation aimed at protecting local governments that reject projects from corporate lawsuits.
  • The fight captures the emerging politics around AI infrastructure: Communities may want the investment and jobs, but they also want control over the costs.

Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

item.title: Trump has a new target: The words Americans use
item.description:
President Trump has long nicknamed his opponents, and now, as November approaches, he's even trying to dictate the vocabulary around key issues.

The big picture: Trump's latest effort to reshape political language follows his longtime political strategy: Define the terms of the debate, and you gain power over the debate itself.

  • But as polling on those issues continues to haunt the president's party, Trump's new vocabulary may not be enough to change voters' minds.

Case in point: Americans are worried about AI — but to Trump, that word no longer exists. It's "super intelligence" now.

  • Voters are also concerned about affordability, but that's a "new word" and a "hoax," Trump says.
  • And the war in Iran? Sometimes Trump says it's a war — a word that carries strict legal implications — and other times it's an "excursion," a "military operation" or a "skirmish."

The intrigue: The issues are starkly different, but the throughline is the way Trump frames the linguistic building blocks of political debate.

  • "If you can actually get everyone who influences our perception of language to adopt your language, you have a very powerful capacity," says Kathleen Hall Jamieson, a communications professor at the University of Pennsylvania and director emerita of the Annenberg Public Policy Center.

What they're saying: "President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress," White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement to Axios.

The latest: As fears about AI's potential threat to humanity (which the president has labeled a "hoax") boiled over, Trump — who has favored a light regulatory touch — signed an executive order replacing "artificial" with a different word: "super."

  • "This is a highly contentious issue right now that is working against him because his position is unpopular," Jamieson says.
  • She adds: "But AI … is so pervasive right now in the news environment and the anxieties of the culture that if you can attach positive affect to it as opposed to negative affect to it, you've accomplished something."
  • The reaction has been mixed: Elon Musk said he'd rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI, but Sam Altman told Politico he wouldn't rename OpenAI, noting that "brands are sticky."

Zoom in: Trump is also fighting an uphill battle against the word "affordability": a simple term for complex economic strain that Democrats harnessed in key elections and have championed throughout the midterm cycle.

  • He's said it's a word the press devised, a "fake word" and a Democratic "con job." But unlike with SI, he hasn't offered an alternative.
  • But he's also leaned on his own midterm buzz words, "communism" being a prime example.

Between the lines: "If you can shape which words are used in a political debate and how those words are defined, then you've won the debate before it even starts," explains Jennifer Mercieca, a Texas A&M professor and author of "Demagogue for President: The Rhetorical Genius of Donald Trump."

  • "President Trump knows this, of course, and has been very successful in re-framing or re-defining issues," she writes to Axios, pointing to his popularization of the term "fake news." But Trump's "frame warfare isn't surprising" as "it is essential to how politics works today."
  • Trump's second administration has expanded that battle over language, renaming the Gulf of Mexico, Lake Ontario and the Department of Defense. Keywords tied to diversity and gender have driven grant cancellations.
  • And with Trump's punitive response to anyone who doesn't use his preferred language, Jamieson says: "You may be adding a function to the presidency, a controversial function, which is namer-in-chief."

The bottom line: Our perceptions can be shaped by language — but the key question for November is whether our elections can be.

Go deeper: Inside Trump's "super intelligence" naming problem

item.title: Missing details keep U.S. plague response on hold
item.description:
Two big unknowns stand in the way of determining how serious the plague threat in Russia is and whether travel advisories, restrictions at U.S. ports of entry or other precautions are warranted.

  • We still don't know which pathogen killed a Russian researcher, or how well contained it is.

Why it matters: Though public health experts say there's no cause for Americans to panic, the episode serves as a wake-up call emphasizing the nature of global biological threats and the need for pandemic preparedness.

State of play: A worker at the Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East recently died after contracting pneumonia. There are conflicting accounts of how she got sick and whether she was infected with pneumonic plague, which is almost always deadly without prompt treatment with antibiotics.

  • Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that the administration is closely monitoring the situation, adding, "I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause to just keep an eye on. And we're doing that."
  • If a response is required, "the playbook for these instances is very well defined," David Mansdoerfer, a former health official in the first Trump administration, told Axios.
  • "Traditionally, the precautionary measures the government would take would be via a travel advisory from [the State Department]," he said, adding the U.S. already has its most serious travel warning in place for Russia due to the war with Ukraine.
  • It would also contact U.S. citizens in the affected area with guidance, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention would follow up with a travel health notice, Mansdoerfer said.
  • "The government would then focus on [Customs and Border Protection] ill traveler rules" that can include stopping high-risk individuals from boarding flights or flagging health officials if they land at a port of entry. At that point, "it becomes a CDC protocol-driven process," he added.

The intrigue: If the Russian worker did die from pneumonic plague, experts say there's a possibility that it was a genetically altered version that behaves differently than the treatable strain.

  • That's just speculation at this point. But the prevalence of "gain-of-function" research that enhances pathogens to study them and Russia's known development of biological weapons make it impossible to rule out.

U.S. preparedness efforts will focus first on getting as much detailed information as possible because officials first need to understand what is going on to prepare for it, said Tom Inglesby, director of the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security.

  • "It's really critical to get the diagnosis right. There are conflicting stories around it," Inglesby said, noting that while there are substantial supplies of antibiotics in government stockpiles and pharmacies, there's still the possibility the strain is resistant to them.

Another key unknown is if pneumonia believed to be linked to plague has spread in the community. So far, reports suggest it's limited to the lab scientist who died while others in the community are under close monitoring. 

  • "Pneumonic plague does not normally cause large outbreaks in modern times, it happens rarely but it's very uncommon," Inglesby said. "If many people in that city do get sick, that would call into question the diagnosis, or raise concerns about something else going on."
  • "Getting the real story, the true facts of the situation out in the open is critical to everything else that follows in the response," he added.

Asked whether he's concerned, President Trump on Monday said: "Somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter. They're like an army ... even with great advances, the germs have really become relatively stronger than they were, and things that used to work on pneumonia don't work as well anymore."

Friction point: Determining whether the incident resulted from legitimate plague research as opposed to a weapons program is important, considering the still-heated debate over COVID's origins and the Russian institute's connection with the nation's biowarfare apparatus.

  • There's no credible evidence that the deceased worker at the Russian institute was involved with research on a weaponized or engineered strain. In fact, some reports state she had recently traveled to regions along the Mongolia-Russia border, where plague naturally occurs in animals.
  • The institute where she worked was established as part of an anti-plague network and was mainly responsible for surveillance of dangerous pathogens. But it developed vaccines and diagnostics for pathogens that were modified by the military, according to the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies.

A 2024 State Department assessment concluded Russia maintains an offensive bioweapons program and absorbed the old Soviet program and evolved it.

  • The CDC says the Soviet Union in the 1970s and 1980s manufactured large quantities of antibiotic-resistant Y. pestis [the bacteria that causes plague] to be dispersed in the air as a bioweapon and that, in light of these and recent events involving terrorist organizations, the United States and other countries must be prepared for a bioterrorism attack involving Y. pestis.

Zoom out: Pneumonic plague cases are rare but not unheard of, including in the U.S.

  • Last year, the CDC launched a pneumonic plague investigation in Arizona after a young adult male died after exposure to two ill cats. Officials identified 46 potentially exposed persons, who were given antibiotics.

The bottom line: In the most optimistic scenario, Russia has responded with an abundance of caution to a one-off deadly infection that hasn't spread.

  • But there's too much that still needs to be verified to draw any conclusions.

item.title: Scoop: Senate GOP to send $5m to shore up Graham in South Carolina
item.description:
The main super PAC supporting Republican Senate candidates plans to inject $5 million into the South Carolina campaign as an "insurance policy" to help GOP nominee Darline Graham, a source familiar with the move tells Axios.

Why it matters: The GOP's concern that a Senate seat in blood-red South Carolina could be in play shows just how bad the political environment is for Republicans, who face a rash of troubles in states long considered conservative strongholds.

  • "It's an insurance policy. We're going to be there for Darline," said a Republican briefed on the plans for the Senate Leadership Fund.

The shift to spending in conservative South Carolina comes after Senate Republicans announced they no longer were financing ads in swing-state North Carolina, where the GOP's Michael Whatley is lagging behind former Gov. Roy Cooper (D) in polls.

  • Democrats, meanwhile, are reallocating resources in a way that reflects their optimism four weeks before Election Day.
  • Democrats' main Senate super PAC canceled roughly $1.1 million in ad reservations in North Carolina, based on their belief Cooper is well-positioned to flip the seat now held by retiring Republican Thom Tillis.

Zoom in: Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, was appointed to her seat in July at the urging of President Trump, a friend of her brother's. Graham faces a host of challenges:

  • She's a relatively poor fundraiser compared to her Democratic opponent, Annie Andrews, a pediatrician who is outspending and outraising Graham, according to the South Carolina Post & Courier.
  • Unlike her brother, Graham shields herself from the press and has shown a relative lack of mastery of foreign policy, which tripped her up during a GOP primary debate.
  • Graham won that primary over Rep. Ralph Norman with 52% of the vote after getting help from Trump. It left some bad feelings with Norman, who endorsed her but briefly suggested he would mount a write-in campaign for the Nov. 3 general election.

Zoom out: Voter anger over high prices and Trump's sagging popularity have helped to create a political landscape in which the Senate Leadership Fund super PAC is having to play defense across the country.

  • It's trying to shore up GOP incumbents and challengers from Alaska to Ohio to Texas, where it recently plowed in $131 million over 17 days to boost Ken Paxton's campaign against Democrat James Talarico.
  • "We're not taking anything for granted. We won't be caught flat-footed in any of these races," the source said.
  • The money for Graham will be spent mainly on TV ads to "remind voters that Andrews is a Democrat."
  • Democrats haven't won a statewide race in South Carolina since 2006.

By the numbers: Closer-than-expected polling from two firms that typically survey for Republicans sparked concern last week in GOP circles.

  • A survey from Trafalgar showed Graham pulling 43% and Andrews 42%, a statistical tie.
  • InsiderAdvantage also produced a poll showing a 1-point race that's essentially tied, with Graham at 46% and Andrews at 45%.
  • Earlier in September, GOP-leaning Rasmussen Reports showed Graham up by 5 points.

Catch up quick: Andrews' campaign has been under the radar compared to that of Jaime Harrison, the Democrat who challenged Graham's brother for the seat in 2020.

  • Harrison raised $100 million for that race, but because he was the state's former Democratic Party chair, it was easier for Republicans to make the race a partisan contest.
  • In contrast, Andrews is running as a "mom and a doctor." Her campaign was largely financed with $3.6 million in campaign contributions bundled by 314 Action Fund, a political committee founded to elect Democratic candidates with STEM backgrounds.

What they're saying: "South Carolinians don't know who Darline Graham is or what she believes — she avoids reporters, avoids voters, and lies about Annie rather than doing her job," an Andrews spokesperson told Axios.

  • A Graham spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.
  • Trump gave a preview Monday of the bare-knuckle attacks to come when he took to Truth Social and used a slur for transgender people to attack Andrews while accusing her of a host of liberal positions.
  • "South Carolina must show, in the upcoming Election, that it is not for her," Trump wrote.

The 314 Action Fund jabbed back at the president in a statement late Monday, calling Trump "perverted" and saying that he "has resorted to name-calling and juvenile insults because his candidate can't win on the issues."

Axios' Hans Nichols contributed to this story.
item.content:encoded:
The main super PAC supporting Republican Senate candidates plans to inject $5 million into the South Carolina campaign as an "insurance policy" to help GOP nominee Darline Graham, a source familiar with the move tells Axios.

Why it matters: The GOP's concern that a Senate seat in blood-red South Carolina could be in play shows just how bad the political environment is for Republicans, who face a rash of troubles in states long considered conservative strongholds.

  • "It's an insurance policy. We're going to be there for Darline," said a Republican briefed on the plans for the Senate Leadership Fund.

The shift to spending in conservative South Carolina comes after Senate Republicans announced they no longer were financing ads in swing-state North Carolina, where the GOP's Michael Whatley is lagging behind former Gov. Roy Cooper (D) in polls.

  • Democrats, meanwhile, are reallocating resources in a way that reflects their optimism four weeks before Election Day.
  • Democrats' main Senate super PAC canceled roughly $1.1 million in ad reservations in North Carolina, based on their belief Cooper is well-positioned to flip the seat now held by retiring Republican Thom Tillis.

Zoom in: Graham, the sister of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, was appointed to her seat in July at the urging of President Trump, a friend of her brother's. Graham faces a host of challenges:

  • She's a relatively poor fundraiser compared to her Democratic opponent, Annie Andrews, a pediatrician who is outspending and outraising Graham, according to the South Carolina Post & Courier.
  • Unlike her brother, Graham shields herself from the press and has shown a relative lack of mastery of foreign policy, which tripped her up during a GOP primary debate.
  • Graham won that primary over Rep. Ralph Norman with 52% of the vote after getting help from Trump. It left some bad feelings with Norman, who endorsed her but briefly suggested he would mount a write-in campaign for the Nov. 3 general election.

Zoom out: Voter anger over high prices and Trump's sagging popularity have helped to create a political landscape in which the Senate Leadership Fund super PAC is having to play defense across the country.

  • It's trying to shore up GOP incumbents and challengers from Alaska to Ohio to Texas, where it recently plowed in $131 million over 17 days to boost Ken Paxton's campaign against Democrat James Talarico.
  • "We're not taking anything for granted. We won't be caught flat-footed in any of these races," the source said.
  • The money for Graham will be spent mainly on TV ads to "remind voters that Andrews is a Democrat."
  • Democrats haven't won a statewide race in South Carolina since 2006.

By the numbers: Closer-than-expected polling from two firms that typically survey for Republicans sparked concern last week in GOP circles.

  • A survey from Trafalgar showed Graham pulling 43% and Andrews 42%, a statistical tie.
  • InsiderAdvantage also produced a poll showing a 1-point race that's essentially tied, with Graham at 46% and Andrews at 45%.
  • Earlier in September, GOP-leaning Rasmussen Reports showed Graham up by 5 points.

Catch up quick: Andrews' campaign has been under the radar compared to that of Jaime Harrison, the Democrat who challenged Graham's brother for the seat in 2020.

  • Harrison raised $100 million for that race, but because he was the state's former Democratic Party chair, it was easier for Republicans to make the race a partisan contest.
  • In contrast, Andrews is running as a "mom and a doctor." Her campaign was largely financed with $3.6 million in campaign contributions bundled by 314 Action Fund, a political committee founded to elect Democratic candidates with STEM backgrounds.

What they're saying: "South Carolinians don't know who Darline Graham is or what she believes — she avoids reporters, avoids voters, and lies about Annie rather than doing her job," an Andrews spokesperson told Axios.

  • A Graham spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.
  • Trump gave a preview Monday of the bare-knuckle attacks to come when he took to Truth Social and used a slur for transgender people to attack Andrews while accusing her of a host of liberal positions.
  • "South Carolina must show, in the upcoming Election, that it is not for her," Trump wrote.

The 314 Action Fund jabbed back at the president in a statement late Monday, calling Trump "perverted" and saying that he "has resorted to name-calling and juvenile insults because his candidate can't win on the issues."

Axios' Hans Nichols contributed to this story.

item.title: Longevity guru Bryan Johnson: "People really want me to die"
item.description:
LOS ANGELES — Bryan Johnson, the face of the longevity movement who believes he may never die, announced recently that he had an incurable autoimmune disease — and his critics cheered, he told "The Axios Show" in an exclusive interview Monday.

  • "I mean, I think people really want me to die. Now I get it. It's funny. It's ironic. I push a lot of buttons that people don't like," he said.

The big picture: As Johnson himself acknowledged, there's an irony in the founder of the "Don't Die" movement watching people celebrate his diagnosis. But Johnson sees his diagnosis as rocket fuel for his mission to promote longevity, rather than a setback.

Catch up quick: Johnson, 49, has autoimmune gastritis (AIG), a chronic condition in which the immune system attacks healthy cells in the stomach lining.

  • Johnson said "there was joy all around the world" after he announced his diagnosis in July.
  • He spends millions of dollars a year on extreme health interventions, documenting the experiments for an online following that has ballooned to roughly 8 million across platforms including YouTube.
  • When asked if any of his interventions could have fueled his AIG diagnosis, he said: "No. I got diagnosed with hypothyroidism when I was 21 years old. The thyroid and the stomach are very closely linked in immunology. I probably have had this thing for about 30 years."

The intrigue: Johnson views the diagnosis, which might appear to undermine his campaign against aging, as just another test of it.

  • In his view, his efforts to do more than manage the disease can help prove the efficacy of his ambitions.
  • "I like the challenge. I'm up for it. I think it's good timing. I'm going to get diagnosed with something at some point. Why not this?"

Friction point: Johnson, who calls himself the "most measured person in the world," spends over $2 million a year on his personal health and longevity treatments. He has an entire medical concierge team and a makeshift doctor's office in his home.

  • Experts say the cause of the disease is unknown, and that Johnson's proposed effort to reverse it is experimental.

Zoom out: Johnson made his fortune founding Braintree, which bought Venmo and was later sold to PayPal for $800 million.

  • He now runs longevity businesses including Blueprint and Immortals, alongside neurotechnology company Kernel and venture fund OS Fund.

Between the lines: One common critique of intensive health tracking is that more testing can uncover more abnormalities, not all of them meaningful.

  • Doctors warn that false positives and incidental findings can trigger a "cascade" of follow-up tests and treatments that can bring added cost, stress, and in some cases, harm.

Johnson is a full-throated fan: "I personally appreciate information. I want to know because when you find things early, you're much more likely to be able to address them."

  • He also said his process doesn't feel addictive to him, adding that "the biggest addiction in the world is to make money."

The bottom line: The face of the longevity movement sees the hit to his public health record as another potential achievement in his quest to live forever.

item.title: Wall Street on track for record profits
item.description:
Data: NYSE/Intercontinental Exchange via the New York State Comptroller; Chart Emily Peck/Axios; Note: 2026 projected by the comptroller if first-half growth continues at current pace. First-half 2026 profits were $45.9 billion. Profits are for broker-dealer operations of NYSE member firms and are not adjusted for inflation.

Wall Street profits are blowing past expectations this year, the New York State Comptroller's office finds in a new report.

Why it matters: Profits are on track for an all-time record, a sign of how the AI boom is fueling dealmaking and how volatile markets are helping trading.

By the numbers: In the first half of this year, Wall Street firms raked in $45.9 billion — that's 51.3% more than the same period last year, and already more than the $45.3 billion forecast for the entirety of 2026.

  • If growth continues apace, annual profits could exceed $90 billion.

Zoom out: That's far more than 2025's record $65.1 billion and rivals the 2009 record even after accounting for inflation, the report says.

Stunning stat: The fees that firms earn from underwriting — helping companies sell new stocks and bonds — rose 68% in the first half of the year, compared with the first half of 2025.

Zoom in: That tracks with a 76.5% increase in global equity issuance, a large chunk from the SpaceX initial public offering.

  • Plus, there was also an 11.3% increase in debt issuance, with the AI hyperscalers among the biggest borrowers.

Yes, but: It's anyone's guess as to whether the second half of the year looks like the first.

  • There are plenty of market headwinds blowing: the Iran war, higher inflation and interest rates, the potential for the AI bubble to burst among them.

The intrigue: Wall Street appears to be thriving despite fears over the city's democratic socialist mayor, Zohran Mamdani.

The big picture: The securities industry makes up a big and growing share of the city and state's tax revenues, but local business and politics aren't significant profit engines.

  • Those instead are driven by national and global markets — it's been a huge year for stocks, the SpaceX IPO was the biggest ever, M&A hit a record and war-driven volatility juiced trading.

What to watch: The big Wall Street banks are set to release third-quarter earnings numbers next week — that's the first big test of whether the pace is holding up.

item.title: Latino group bets on bilingual AI to cut voter confusion before the midterms
item.description:
A national Latino civic engagement group is turning to an AI app to help voters cut through an increasingly complicated election system — in English or Spanish.

Why it matters: Nearly 39 million Hispanics can vote in this year's midterms, and their political loyalties are increasingly up for grabs.

  • Hispanics have added 5.25 million eligible voters since 2022, more than any other racial or ethnic group, according to Pew Research Center.
  • The Latino electorate remains highly fluid: About 1 in 7 Latino voters who backed Trump in 2024 now say they want Democrats to control Congress, according to a new NBC News/Telemundo poll.

How it works: Mi Familia en Acción launched Nubi last week, a bilingual AI-powered app that answers questions about voting, voter registration, citizenship and Know Your Rights information.

  • Users can ask questions in English or Spanish about where and when to vote, early voting, mail ballots and registration.
  • Nubi operates in all 50 states and can tailor information to the local or district level.

Unlike a general-purpose chatbot, Mi Familia en Acción president and CEO Héctor Sánchez Barba tells Axios that Nubi doesn't search the open internet for answers.

  • The organization feeds it information from sources it considers reliable, with human review and guardrails around what the AI can answer.
  • If Nubi doesn't have an answer, Sánchez said, it is designed to say so and direct the user to a trusted source or partner rather than invent a response.

State of play: Nubi represents a five-year effort to marry Mi Familia en Acción's traditional organizing with technology.

  • The organization launched a more basic chatbot about two years ago before developing the current AI version.
  • Mi Familia en Acción financed development itself, Sánchez said, though he declined to disclose the cost, calling it a "very big investment."
  • The organization says it plans to keep updating Nubi as voting rules, court decisions and government policies change.

Zoom in: The goal is to turn a complicated search across election websites into a conversation.

  • A voter could ask whether they're registered, whether they can vote by mail, where their polling place is or what early-voting options exist.
  • Nubi then walks the user through basic questions before giving a locally specific answer.
  • The tool is updated regularly and eventually could expand its answers on questions involving immigration enforcement or problems a voter encounters at a polling place.

What they're saying: "People don't need to be a constitutional lawyer to find information about how they need to vote," said Sánchez, adding that the goal is to put reliable information in one place.

  • He stressed that Nubi is nonpartisan and doesn't recommend candidates or causes.
  • Sánchez also said the technology won't replace door-knocking and other traditional organizing, but could extend civic information into rural or overlooked communities that organizers rarely reach.

Zoom out: Nubi arrives as Latino voters play an increasingly large — and less predictable — role in American elections.

  • Pew projects Hispanics will account for 16% of eligible voters in 2026, nearly double their 9% share in 2006.
  • Latino voters are also fragmenting into competing political identities rather than moving uniformly toward either party.
  • In May, 52% of registered Latino voters surveyed in 17 competitive House districts said they were undecided or could change their minds.
